subject: math
cluster: Reason quantitatively and use units to solve problems
intro: Modeling starts by deciding what to measure. For each item, define the quantity (or quantities) with an appropriate unit, choose the right type of quantity (count, total, rate, ratio, per-capita figure, or percent), and make sure your quantity is measurable and aligned with the question being asked. Many items have more than one acceptable response; the answer key gives a strong model answer and explains what makes it correct.

items.prompt: A coach wants to record how far each runner ran during a $30$-minute practice. Name one quantity, with its unit, that the coach should measure for each runner.
items.answer: Distance run, measured in miles (or meters/kilometers).

steps: The question asks how far each runner ran, so the quantity to measure is distance.
Distance is reported in a length unit: miles, kilometers, or meters.
A conventional, well defined answer is distance run in miles, for example $2.5$ miles.

items.prompt: A driver wants to describe how fast a car is traveling on a highway. State the appropriate quantity and its conventional unit.
items.answer: Speed, measured in miles per hour (mph).

steps: How fast something travels is a speed, which is distance divided by time.
The conventional unit for highway speed is miles per hour, written mph.
So the quantity is speed measured in miles per hour, for example $65$ mph. A length unit alone, such as miles, would not capture speed.

items.prompt: A store manager wants to track how many customers enter the shop each day. Name the quantity and its unit.
items.answer: A daily customer count, measured in customers per day (people per day).

steps: Tracking how many customers arrive is a count.
Because it is measured over each day, the unit is customers per day.
A well defined answer is the number of customers per day, for example $480$ customers per day.

items.prompt: A nurse needs a quantity to describe a patient's body temperature for a health model. State the quantity, a sensible unit, and a sensible level of precision (to the nearest what?).
items.answer: Body temperature in degrees Fahrenheit, reported to the nearest tenth of a degree (for example $98.6^\circ\text{F}$).

steps: The quantity is body temperature.
A conventional clinical unit is degrees Fahrenheit ($^\circ\text{F}$); degrees Celsius is also acceptable.

Clinical thermometers read to the nearest tenth of a degree, so a sensible precision is the nearest $0.1^\circ\text{F}$, for example $98.6^\circ\text{F}$. Reporting to the nearest whole degree loses useful detail, and to the nearest thousandth is unrealistic.

items.prompt: A cashier earns money by the hour. To build a model of weekly earnings, name the rate quantity the cashier must know and give its unit.
items.answer: An hourly wage (pay rate), measured in dollars per hour.

steps: Weekly earnings depend on how much the cashier is paid for each hour worked, which is a rate.
The unit of a pay rate is dollars per hour, written $\$/\text{hour}$.
So the quantity is the hourly wage, for example $\$16$ per hour. Multiplying this rate by hours worked gives weekly earnings.

items.prompt: Country $A$ produces $1{,}200{,}000$ tons of wheat and Country $B$ produces $400{,}000$ tons. To judge which country is more agriculturally productive per worker, explain why comparing total tons is misleading, then define a better quantity with its unit.
items.answer: Define wheat produced per farm worker, measured in tons per worker; comparing raw totals ignores that the countries may have very different numbers of workers.

steps: Raw totals favor whichever country is simply bigger or has more workers, so they do not measure productivity per worker.
Productivity is a rate: output divided by the number of workers producing it.
Define the quantity as wheat produced per farm worker, with unit tons per worker (tons/worker).

For example, if Country $A$ has $300{,}000$ farm workers and Country $B$ has $80{,}000$, then $A$ produces $\frac{1{,}200{,}000}{300{,}000}=4$ tons/worker and $B$ produces $\frac{400{,}000}{80{,}000}=5$ tons/worker, so $B$ is more productive even though its total is smaller.

items.prompt: A city manager compares water use across neighborhoods of very different sizes. Should water use be reported as total gallons per month or as gallons per person per day? Name the better quantity and give a one-sentence justification.
items.answer: Gallons per person per day, because it adjusts for population so neighborhoods of different sizes can be compared fairly.

steps: Total gallons per month will be large simply because a neighborhood has more people, not because each person uses more water.
A fair comparison across differently sized groups requires a per-capita rate.
Define the quantity as gallons per person per day (a per-capita daily rate), which isolates how much water a typical individual uses regardless of neighborhood size.

items.prompt: A teacher wants to compare how well two classes did on a test. Class $1$ had $24$ of $30$ students pass and Class $2$ had $18$ of $20$ students pass. Explain why comparing the number who passed is unfair, and define the quantity that allows a valid comparison.
items.answer: Define the percent (or fraction) of students who passed in each class; comparing raw counts is unfair because the classes have different sizes.

steps: Class $1$ has more students, so it can have more passers even if a smaller share passed; a raw count ignores class size.
To compare fairly, convert to a percent of students who passed in each class.
So the quantity is the pass percentage, and Class $2$ did better ($90\%$ vs. $80\%$) even though fewer students passed in total.

items.prompt: To compare two streaming services, a student proposes the quantity 'number of good movies.' Explain why this quantity is not well defined for a model, and define a measurable quantity that could replace it.
items.answer: 'Good' is subjective, so two people cannot measure it and agree; replace it with a measurable quantity such as the number of titles rated $4$ stars or higher by users (a count), or the percent of a service's catalog rated above a fixed threshold.

steps: A quantity is operationally well defined only if two observers following the same procedure would get the same value.
'Good' has no agreed cutoff, so different people would count different movies; the quantity is not measurable as stated.
Fix it by attaching a measurable rule, for example: the number of titles with an average user rating of at least $4$ out of $5$ stars.
This replacement is a count (unit: titles) that anyone can reproduce from the rating data, so it is well defined.

items.prompt: A school wants to know whether its cafeteria is too crowded at lunch. A student suggests using 'total number of students enrolled' as the quantity. Explain why that quantity is off target, and define a better quantity with its unit.
items.answer: Enrollment counts everyone in the school, not how packed the cafeteria is at one time; a better quantity is the number of students per square foot (or per seat) in the cafeteria during lunch.

steps: Total enrollment includes students who are not in the cafeteria and ignores the room's size, so it does not measure crowdedness.
Crowdedness is about how many people occupy a fixed space at once, which is a density.
Define the quantity as students per square foot of cafeteria floor (or students per available seat) during the lunch period.
For example $0.15$ students per square foot during lunch directly captures how packed the room is, which enrollment cannot.

items.prompt: You are choosing between two cell phone plans. Plan $X$ costs $\$30$ per month plus $\$0.10$ per GB of data; Plan $Y$ costs $\$45$ per month with unlimited data. List the quantities, with units, you must define to model total yearly cost as a function of monthly data use $d$, and write the yearly cost of Plan $X$ as a formula in $d$.
items.answer: Define $d$ = monthly data use in GB per month, the monthly fee in dollars per month, and the per-GB charge in dollars per GB; then yearly cost of Plan $X$ is $C_X(d)=12(30+0.10d)=360+1.2d$ dollars per year.

steps: Identify the variable quantity: monthly data use $d$, measured in GB per month.
Identify the constant quantities: a monthly fee in dollars per month and a per-GB charge in dollars per GB.
Plan $X$ monthly cost is the fee plus the per-GB charge times data: $30+0.10d$ dollars per month.
Yearly cost multiplies the monthly cost by $12$ months: $C_X(d)=12(30+0.10d)=360+1.2d$ dollars per year.
Each term carries consistent units: $\$0.10/\text{GB} \times d\,\text{GB} = \$0.10d$ per month, times $12$ months gives $\$1.2d$ per year.

items.prompt: A model estimates the average speed of cars on a residential street to help set a speed limit. State an appropriate unit, a sensible level of precision (to the nearest what?), and a reasonable range of values the quantity could take. Then explain why a precision of 'the nearest thousandth of a mile per hour' is inappropriate.
items.answer: Average speed in miles per hour, reported to the nearest $1$ mph (or $0.1$ mph), with a reasonable range of roughly $0$ to $45$ mph on a residential street; thousandth-mph precision is meaningless because measurement error far exceeds that.

steps: The quantity is average car speed, with unit miles per hour (mph).
Radar and speed studies are reliable only to about a whole mph, so a sensible precision is the nearest $1$ mph (or at most $0.1$ mph).
On a residential street, speeds realistically range from near $0$ mph (stopped) up to about $40$ to $45$ mph, so a reasonable range is $0$ to $45$ mph.
Reporting to the nearest thousandth of a mph claims precision far smaller than the measurement error, so those digits are noise and not meaningful.

items.prompt: A city wants to decide which of two neighborhoods is more crowded. Neighborhood $P$ has $9{,}000$ residents on $3$ square miles; Neighborhood $Q$ has $12{,}000$ residents on $6$ square miles. Define the quantity that answers the question, give its unit, compute it for each, and explain why comparing total population would give the wrong answer.
items.answer: Define population density = residents per square mile (people/mi$^2$); $P$ has $\frac{9000}{3}=3000$ people/mi$^2$ and $Q$ has $\frac{12000}{6}=2000$ people/mi$^2$, so $P$ is more crowded, while comparing totals would wrongly pick $Q$.

steps: Crowdedness compares people to the area they occupy, so define population density = residents divided by area, with unit people per square mile.
Neighborhood $P$: $\frac{9{,}000\ \text{people}}{3\ \text{mi}^2}=3{,}000$ people/mi$^2$.
Neighborhood $Q$: $\frac{12{,}000\ \text{people}}{6\ \text{mi}^2}=2{,}000$ people/mi$^2$.
By density, $P$ ($3{,}000$) is more crowded than $Q$ ($2{,}000$).
Total population would pick $Q$ ($12{,}000 > 9{,}000$), but that ignores area and so answers the wrong question.

items.prompt: A bakery wants to model its daily profit. Define a coherent set of at least three quantities, each with a unit, needed to express daily profit, then write profit as an equation relating them.
items.answer: Let $n$ = loaves sold per day (loaves/day), $p$ = price per loaf ($\$/\text{loaf}$), $c$ = cost per loaf ($\$/\text{loaf}$), and $F$ = fixed daily cost ($\$/\text{day}$); then daily profit $P = (p-c)\,n - F$ dollars per day.

steps: Profit is revenue minus total cost, so define the quantities that build each part.
Revenue depends on loaves sold per day, $n$ (loaves/day), and price per loaf, $p$ ($\$/\text{loaf}$): revenue $= pn$ dollars per day.
Variable cost depends on cost to make each loaf, $c$ ($\$/\text{loaf}$): variable cost $= cn$; fixed daily cost $F$ ($\$/\text{day}$) covers rent and utilities.
Combine: daily profit $P = pn - cn - F = (p-c)\,n - F$, with unit dollars per day.
Every term carries dollars-per-day units, so the equation is dimensionally consistent.

items.prompt: Two delivery companies want to compare fuel efficiency across their fleets. Company $M$ proposes 'total gallons of fuel used last year' as the quantity; Company $N$ proposes 'miles driven per gallon, averaged over the fleet.' Decide which quantity better answers the efficiency question, justify the unit, and explain the flaw in the rejected quantity.
items.answer: Miles per gallon (mi/gal), averaged over the fleet, is the better quantity; total gallons used measures volume of consumption, not efficiency, and is biased by how much each fleet drives.

steps: Efficiency means how much output (distance) you get per unit of fuel, which is a rate.
Miles per gallon (mi/gal) is exactly that rate, so it directly measures efficiency and its unit, distance per volume, is appropriate.
Total gallons used is just a volume; a company that drives more will burn more fuel even if every truck is highly efficient, so the total is biased by fleet size and mileage.
Therefore define fleet-average miles per gallon as the quantity; Company $N$'s choice answers the efficiency question and Company $M$'s does not.
